name: natural numbers
essential_semantics: An inductive type of counting numbers with a declared convention on whether 0 is included, closed under + and *, not under subtraction.
rationale: Indices, cardinalities and induction all live on N; conflating it with the integers loses the induction principle and the non-negativity guarantee.

name: integers
essential_semantics: Ring of signed whole numbers with exact arithmetic and no rounding; distinct from a fixed-width machine integer.
rationale: Exactness is semantic: an integer that silently wraps at 2^64 is a different mathematical object.

name: rationals
essential_semantics: Field of exact fractions, with equality up to reduction, not represented as a float.
rationale: The exact/inexact boundary is where most mathematical software silently lies; rationals are the canonical exact non-integer domain.

name: real numbers
essential_semantics: Complete ordered field treated as an idealised mathematical object, explicitly distinct from any floating-point approximation of it.
rationale: Almost all analysis, probability and physics is stated over R; identifying R with float64 is a category error with measurable consequences.

name: complex numbers
essential_semantics: Algebraically closed field with conjugation, modulus and argument; ordering must be absent (no < on C).
canonical_example: e^{i theta} = cos theta + i sin theta
rationale: Eigenvalues, Fourier analysis and quantum formalism need C; permitting < on complex numbers is a detectable soundness failure.

name: extended reals with +/- infinity
essential_semantics: R together with two infinities, with the indeterminate forms left undefined rather than given arbitrary values.
canonical_example: sup of an unbounded set is +infinity; infinity - infinity is undefined
rationale: Measure theory and optimisation routinely take values in the extended reals; treating infinity as a float sentinel destroys the distinction.

name: non-negative reals
essential_semantics: Refinement of R by x >= 0, closed under addition and multiplication but not subtraction.
rationale: Measures, norms, variances and distances are non-negative by construction; carrying that in the type prevents whole classes of nonsense.

name: strictly positive reals
essential_semantics: Refinement by x > 0, closed under multiplication and division; the domain on which log is total.
rationale: Scale parameters, rates and bandwidths are strictly positive; the strict/non-strict distinction changes which operations are total.

name: unit interval [0,1]
essential_semantics: Refinement of R to [0,1], closed under multiplication and convex combination but not under addition.
canonical_example: p in [0,1] as a Bernoulli parameter
rationale: Probabilities and mixture weights live here; a type that permits p1 + p2 to escape [0,1] without comment is unsound for probability.

name: probability-valued scalar distinct from generic magnitude
essential_semantics: A value carrying the semantics of a probability (normalisation, complement, product-under-independence) rather than merely a number in [0,1].
rationale: A probability and a positive magnitude are not interchangeable even when numerically equal; the complement operation is meaningful for one and not the other.

name: intervals as domains
essential_semantics: Open, closed and half-open intervals with endpoint inclusion recorded, usable as quantification and integration domains.
rationale: The open/closed endpoint distinction is load-bearing in analysis theorems and is routinely lost when intervals are stored as bare pairs.

name: integers modulo n
essential_semantics: Quotient ring Z/nZ with residue classes as objects and congruence as the equality.
rationale: Number theory and cryptography require it, and it is the simplest quotient structure that stresses the quotient machinery.

name: congruence and modular relations
essential_semantics: The relation a is congruent to b mod n as a proposition, distinct from the mod operator returning a residue.
rationale: Congruence as a relation and mod as a function are different objects; many systems only provide the latter.

name: divisibility relation
essential_semantics: The proposition d divides n, not the division operation.
rationale: Elementary number theory is stated with divisibility; expressing it only as n % d == 0 conflates a relation with a computation.

name: primality
essential_semantics: A predicate on integers with the standard definition, usable inside quantified statements.
rationale: The canonical test of whether a predicate can be defined and quantified over an infinite discrete domain.

name: gcd and lcm
essential_semantics: Greatest common divisor / least common multiple defined by their universal properties over the divisibility order, not merely by an algorithm.
rationale: Included because it distinguishes definition-by-property from definition-by-procedure.

name: total order on numeric domains
essential_semantics: Strict and non-strict comparison with the correct availability per domain (present on R, absent on C), and chained comparisons unambiguously parsed.
rationale: Inequalities are the most common mathematical constraint; ambiguous chained comparison is a real parsing hazard.

name: absolute value and modulus
essential_semantics: A map to non-negative reals, defined uniformly for R and C, with the triangle inequality as a stated property.
rationale: The epsilon-delta idiom is written with absolute value; it is the base case of norms and metrics.

name: sign function and signed reasoning
essential_semantics: A three-valued sign with sign(0) defined by convention, and sign-based case reasoning.
rationale: Small but a common source of convention drift at zero, which a representation should pin down.

name: floor, ceiling and rounding
essential_semantics: Maps from R to Z with the tie-breaking convention explicit for rounding.
rationale: Discretisation steps depend on these, and unspecified tie-breaking is a genuine reproducibility hazard.

name: exact versus approximate value distinction
essential_semantics: The representation records whether a numeral denotes an exact quantity or an approximation, and does not silently promote one to the other.
rationale: Losing exactness silently is the most common way numerical systems produce authoritative-looking wrong statements.

name: declared coercion / promotion policy
essential_semantics: Which numeric embeddings are automatic (N into Z into Q into R into C) and which require an explicit, possibly lossy, cast is specified and enforced.
canonical_example: Real to Integer requires explicit rounding; Integer to Real is automatic
rationale: Undeclared coercion is how type systems leak; the policy is a semantic commitment and must be inspectable.

name: algebraic numbers and radicals
essential_semantics: Numbers presented as roots of polynomials, with branch selection made explicit.
rationale: Exact symbolic answers need it, and unstated branch choice for radicals is a genuine ambiguity.

name: named mathematical constants
essential_semantics: pi, e, gamma etc. as exact symbolic constants, not as their decimal approximations.
canonical_example: integral over R of e^{-x^2} dx = sqrt(pi)
rationale: Closed-form results are stated with symbolic constants; substituting decimals loses exactness and blocks symbolic simplification.

name: cardinality, finiteness and countability
essential_semantics: Size of a set as a cardinal, with finite / countably infinite / uncountable distinguished.
rationale: Discrete versus continuous distributions, countable additivity, and summation versus integration all hinge on cardinality.

name: ordinals and transfinite indexing
essential_semantics: Well-ordered indices beyond the naturals supporting transfinite induction.
canonical_example: the Borel hierarchy indexed by countable ordinals
rationale: Rarely needed outside set theory and descriptive set theory, but the natural completion of the indexing story.

name: numeric vector with declared length
essential_semantics: A finite indexed tuple of scalars whose length is part of its type and whose element type is uniform.
rationale: Parameter vectors, data points and decision variables are all length-typed vectors; untyped lists lose conformability.

name: unambiguous numeric literal syntax
essential_semantics: Literals are parsed with a determinate type and value, including scientific notation, and no locale-dependent reading.
canonical_example: 1e-3 is the real 0.001, not a name
rationale: Surface-level but non-negotiable: literal ambiguity makes every downstream semantic claim unverifiable.

name: quaternions and non-commutative scalars
essential_semantics: A scalar-like domain where multiplication is not commutative, forcing the representation to respect operand order.
rationale: A cheap stress test for whether the system assumes commutativity of multiplication everywhere.

name: p-adic and alternative completions
essential_semantics: A completion of Q under a non-archimedean absolute value, with its own notion of nearness.
rationale: Included as a deliberate low-weight probe of whether 'the reals' are hard-wired as the only completion.
